_metadata.purpose: Maps common Fulfulde security/fraud-related terms to their canonical English keyword equivalents, for use in multilingual scam/threat detection.
_metadata.disclaimer: IMPORTANT: this file has notably lower vocabulary coverage and confidence than hausa.json, yoruba.json, igbo.json, and swahili.json. Fulfulde/Fula is spoken across a very wide dialect continuum (Nigeria, Senegal, Guinea, Mali, Cameroon and more), and accessible documentation of tech/security-specific vocabulary is far sparser online than for the other four languages. Only 2 entries below (ceede=money, gujjo=thief) were confirmed against an actual dictionary/source text this session; nearly everything else is either a common loanword pattern or an educated inference by analogy to neighboring languages (especially Hausa, given close contact in Northern Nigeria), clearly marked as such. This file needs native-speaker review more than the other three, and should be treated as a minimal starting point, not a finished glossary.

confidence_levels.verified: Cross-checked against a published Fulfulde-English dictionary/source text.
confidence_levels.common: A loanword pattern consistent with how neighboring/contact languages (Hausa, English) handle the same modern/technical concept; not independently dictionary-confirmed this session.
confidence_levels.uncertain: An educated inference (e.g. derived by regular grammatical pattern from a verified word, or by analogy to a related language) rather than a confirmed term; needs native-speaker review before relying on it.

notes: Fulfulde has a large, complex noun-class system (20+ classes) with consonant alternation between related words (e.g. gujjo 'thief' and the verb root for 'to steal' likely share a 'g/w' alternating root). Only a minimal, cautious stopword list is included below rather than attempting to enumerate this system without strong source support.

Most modern/technical vocabulary below (bank, computer, internet, password, malware, phishing, scam) is given as a loanword, following the same pattern seen in Hausa and other regional languages, since no confirmed native Fulfulde coinage for these concepts was found. This is a reasonable real-world assumption (code-switching with Hausa/English for modern terms is extremely common in Northern Nigeria) but is explicitly a lower-confidence guess, not a sourced fact.

stopwords.am: 'I/me' — first person singular pronoun (community knowledge, not independently sourced this session).
stopwords.ko: Focus/topic marker ('that/what/it is'), very common in Fula grammar.

ceede.note: Confirmed via a Western Niger Fulfulde-English dictionary entry.

gujjo.note: Confirmed via a genuine Fulfulde proverb text using the word in context.

wujjude.note: Inferred, not independently confirmed: Fulfulde infinitives commonly end in -ude, and 'gujjo' (thief) plausibly shares a g/w-alternating root with a verb for 'to steal'. Needs native-speaker confirmation.

wujjaa.note: Inferred past/passive form of wujjude; needs native-speaker confirmation.

telefon.note: Loanword, widely used across West African languages for 'telephone'.

banki.note: Loanword, same form used in Hausa and other regional languages.

akaawun.note: Guessed phonetic loanword adaptation of 'account'; not confirmed.

malware.note: Loanword; no confirmed native term found.

phishing.note: Loanword; no confirmed native term found.

scam.note: Loanword; no confirmed native term found.

fraud.note: Loanword; no confirmed native term found.

hack.note: Loanword/code-switching, no confirmed native term found.

kompiyuta.note: Guessed loanword adaptation by analogy to Hausa 'kwamfuta'; not confirmed.

ɓe njiyaa koodii ngam noddii am.english: they asked for my verification code
